newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Co-op awaits predator's next move.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Co-op awaits predator's next move.

text.p: Britain's

Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS)was on Friday waiting for Lanica Trust Plc, which has been stalking the mutual group, to make its next move amid rumours a bid was imminent. British newspapers said Regan was about to make a 1.0 billion pound ($1.6 billion) bid for the non-food businesses of the CWS, ranging from funeral parlours and travel agencies to large farms and the profitable Co-operative Bank.

Entrepreneur Andrew Regan, who heads Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, has given little away about his game-plan since an announcement in February that a company linked to Lanica had made an approach to the CWS.
He has appointed Hambros Bank to advise on his takeover bid, although a spokeswoman for the British merchant bank declined to comment. CWS is being advised by SBC Warburg's Brian Keelan.

Regan's attempt to break-up the CWS is widely viewed as the result of recent poor performances by the multi-billion pound turnover co-operative group, which on Monday reported a fall in 1996 pre-tax profits.
"After the CWS results it was logical that he (Regan) would have to make his move sometime this week," one source told Reuters.
Neither side would comment after a CWS statement on Thursday announced the suspension of two senior executives and an investigation into their dealings with firms controlled by 31-year-old Regan.

The CWS said the suspensions of Allan Green, controller of retailing and David Chambers, chief general manager for buying, marketing and the supply chain, "arose from a suspected recent serious breach of trust".
It has appointed City law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants KPMG to investigate business dealings between areas of CWS managed by the two executives and companies controlled by Regan.
On Monday CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth reiterated the group's stance of not selling any of its businesses to "an asset-stripping middleman".

Melmoth said it was questionable whether Lanica's shares, which have been suspended since February 10, would ever be relisted. The shares were star performers during 1996 and were suspended at 19.5 pounds each.
But analysts said it would not be easy for Lanica to make a bid because of CWS' complex ownership.
"There's no obvious mechanism for a hostile bid for the Co-op to proceed because of its complicated structure," said one, who declined to be named.
But they did not discount the possibility that Regan and his advisors had found a way around this obstacle.

"I think Regan must have had a proper look and evaluated the possibilities. Maybe he has found a way round," he added. And even if his bid does materialise but fails, it would open the way for others who may have some of the Co-op's more lucrative businesses in their sights.
"If Regan gets to the stage where he makes a formal offer, he won't get past first base. But it might flush out some other contenders."
Whatever the outcome, analysts were in no doubt that the episode was putting huge pressure on the Co-op to take drastic action to improve its performance.
"What it does do is put pressure on the Co-op. It knows it has to do something."
Analysts suggested that this would include cutting the number of individual societies from a current 51 to one or two and consolidating its wide-ranging business interests.
"But the Co-op wants to decide what (to sell) and to whom," one analyst said.
